ROOT_CAUSE: The audit question was not 'are the fields filled in' but 'can the claim be checked against something the runtime did not write'. The runtime writes BOTH the episode and the ledger, so their agreement is self-consistency, not proof. Two things had to be true for a real audit to exist: (a) an independent artefact with per-execution granularity, and (b) a sound way to attribute its entries to steps. Both were established by measurement before any rule was written. (a) The MAA framework log learning/maa_logs/maafw.log (27578 lines, 2026-09-14 to 2026-09-16) records every click and key press with coordinates and millisecond timestamps in LOCAL time, while episodes and the ledger are UTC -- an 8 h offset that has to be removed for any join. (b) Attribution must be one-to-one: consecutive steps on this machine are ~2.5 s apart, so a plain +-5 s window around a row swallows the NEXT row's action. Measured: the ADB SELECT_INTEL_PIN ledger row at 13:35:14.866 absorbed the MAA PostClickKey at 13:35:17.660, which is the BACK row's own action at 13:35:17.711. That produced six phantom 'ADB step also drove via MAA' double-drive suspicions. Nearest-row assignment removed all six.
PATCH_SUMMARY: No production code and no historical record was touched, deliberately: the one defect found is a persisted-schema ambiguity and changing a written ledger key is a decision that should not be taken inside a 60-minute audit. What was delivered is a tool that makes the gap visible and a test that stops it from being closed the wrong way. tools/cq_backend_truth.py applies five rules to every recent episode with a backend claim: LEDGER_ROW (match within a measured 20 s, because the episode lags the action by 2-13 s, median 9.6 s over 48 paired steps -- a 3 s window rejected rows that demonstrably exist), LEDGER_AGREES (action and recognition backends agree exactly; executed agrees), FRAMES_ON_DISK (the named before/after screenshots exist), INDEPENDENT_TRACE (an MAA/HYBRID claim must have a MaaController click or key press assigned to its own row, and an ADB claim must not), and NOT_SILENT (a conflict is printed as a conflict). It also reports SEMANTIC_COLLISION separately from CONFLICT, because one of the apparent conflicts is not a disagreement about a fact.
TEST_RESULT: tests/test_backend_truth_audit.py: 6 passed in 0.07 s. It pins both rules that were wrong on the first pass: that an MAA event is credited to exactly one row (with the measured 13:35 boundary case as the counter-example), and that episode.capture_backend and ledger.capture_backend must not be compared as one fact -- the test asserts the wrong comparison is ABSENT from the source, so a future 'fix' that makes the two values equal to silence the report fails.
REPLAY_RESULT: Ran over the last 80 episodes: 68 carry a backend claim, 280 MAA click/key events in the framework log, 160 of them assigned to a ledger row. Result: 6 conflicts, all of them one kind, NO_LEDGER_ROW. Every MAA/HYBRID claim was verified against the framework log and carries the coordinates of the click that was actually issued, e.g. 2026-09-16T02:04:04Z OPEN_INTEL HYBRID -> click=(666, 954) (the row the recalibrated matcher found) and 2026-09-15T09:32:10Z OPEN_INTEL HYBRID -> click=(666, 861) (the older HUD layout). No ADB claim had an MAA event attributed to it once attribution was one-to-one.
LIVE_DETAIL: No live interaction, by design: the order's live_plan says to reuse the episodes this round already produced rather than click again, and the runtime's own goal verifiers are not involved in this question.
BEFORE: Recent backend fields were 100% complete, which was the previous round's metric. Nothing checked whether a MAA/HYBRID claim corresponded to anything outside the runtime, and nothing could attribute a framework-log entry to a specific step.
AFTER: 68 claims audited; every MAA/HYBRID claim traceable to a specific MaaController click or key press on its own row, with coordinates; 6 untraceable claims reported explicitly instead of passing on completeness.
VERIFIER_RESULT: not applicable - no live step; the audit's own contract is the acceptance
REMAINING_ISSUE: SEMANTIC_COLLISION (34 steps, the main finding). ``capture_backend`` is the same name for two different facts: runtime.py:346 writes the OBSERVATION device (which channel produced this episode's frames) and executor_router.py:401 writes the EXECUTOR's device (which device the backend that ran was wired to). They differ exactly when those differ, i.e. on every HYBRID step -- 34 of them here, all with ledger.used_backend=ADB and episode.capture_backend=MAA_MUMU_EXTRAS. Neither value is wrong; the name is. So a reader of either artefact alone cannot tell which channel produced a step's frames. Recommended one-line fix for Codex to approve: ledger.capture_backend is fully determined by ledger.used_backend (ADB->ADB_EXEC_OUT, MAA->MAA_MUMU_EXTRAS) and therefore carries no information the ledger does not already have, so the key can simply be dropped and the audit can read frame provenance from the episode, where the field already answers its own question. Not applied here because it changes a written schema and old rows would keep the old key.

NO_LEDGER_ROW (6 episodes: 2026-09-15T12:43:15/12:43:29/12:43:56/12:44:10/12:59:36/15:16:47). These are not older than the ledger -- the ledger starts 2026-09-14T13:11:34Z and ZERO claims predate it -- so the cause is coverage, not age: those steps ran on a path where no MAA adapter was attached, and build_router returns the plain ADB executor unchanged in that case, so nothing appends a ledger row. A claim made on that path can never be cross-checked. Worth an explicit 'no router' marker in the episode so the absence is stated rather than inferred.

The 20 s and 5 s tolerances are measured on this machine's timings (episode lags action by 2-13 s, median 9.6 s). They are printed in the report so a different machine's numbers are visible rather than assumed.
